title: Professional Conflict Resolution: Language, Strategy, and Principled Negotiation
objectives: Analyse the linguistic strategies used to de-escalate professional conflict without conceding substantive ground
Construct a principled, interest-based response to workplace disagreement that separates positions from underlying needs
Evaluate the ethical dimensions of professional conflict — distinguishing constructive challenge from interpersonal aggression
Synthesise communication research to deploy tentative language, active listening signals, and reframing techniques in high-stakes workplace disputes

authentic_text.title: Memorandum: Proposed Resolution Framework — Project Gamma Dispute
authentic_text.text:
To: All Project Gamma Stakeholders
From: Dispute Resolution Office
Re: Proposed Resolution Framework — Project Gamma Resourcing Dispute

This memorandum sets out a proposed framework for resolving the ongoing dispute between the Technology Division and the Operations Division regarding resourcing allocation on Project Gamma. It is issued in the spirit of constructive dialogue and does not represent a determination of any party's position.

Background:
Following the initial escalation on 14 February, both divisions submitted formal position statements outlining their respective resourcing requirements. An independent review of both submissions has identified that while the stated positions of the two parties appear irreconcilable, the underlying interests they seek to protect are substantially overlapping: both divisions are primarily concerned with ensuring project continuity, managing stakeholder risk, and demonstrating departmental capability within a constrained budget cycle.

Proposed Framework:
Rather than adjudicating between the submitted positions, this office proposes a structured facilitated dialogue in which each division articulates not their resource demands, but the operational outcomes they are seeking to protect. Experience from comparable disputes suggests that when parties shift from positional bargaining to interest-based discussion, the range of viable solutions expands considerably.

Both parties are invited to nominate a representative to attend a facilitated session on 8 March. Participation is voluntary; however, failure to engage with this process will be noted in the event that the dispute requires further escalation.

The goal of this office is not to impose a resolution but to create the conditions in which one can be found.

Principles Governing the Facilitated Dialogue:
The facilitated session will be conducted in accordance with three principles, to which participants are asked to consent in advance. First, the discussion will proceed on an interest-based rather than a positional footing; participants will be asked to articulate the outcomes they seek to protect rather than to restate their resource demands. Second, contributions made during the session will be treated as exploratory and without prejudice, so that no proposal offered in the spirit of problem-solving may later be cited as a concession of position. Third, the facilitator's role is expressly non-adjudicative; the facilitator will not determine the merits of either party's case, but will assist the parties in identifying options that neither, acting alone, might have generated.

Confidentiality and Good Faith:
It is a condition of the process that the substance of the facilitated discussion remain confidential to the participants and to this office, save for any resolution the parties agree may be recorded. This condition is intended to create the conditions for candour: parties are more willing to explore accommodations, and to acknowledge the legitimacy of an opposing interest, where they are assured that doing so will not be used against them should the matter escalate. Participation is expected to be undertaken in good faith, which is understood to mean a genuine willingness to explore mutually acceptable outcomes, not merely attendance for the purpose of demonstrating procedural compliance.

Timeline and Next Steps:
Nominations of representatives are requested by 1 March. The facilitated session is scheduled for 8 March, with a proposed duration of half a day. Should the session produce an agreed framework, that framework will be documented and circulated to both divisions for confirmation within five working days. Should the session not produce agreement, this office will prepare a summary of the areas of convergence and divergence identified, which will inform any subsequent escalation.

Note on Precedent:
The adoption of this interest-based approach is consistent with the resolution of two comparable inter-divisional disputes in the preceding eighteen months, in each of which a facilitated, interest-based dialogue produced a durable agreement that positional escalation had previously failed to achieve. While each dispute is distinct, the pattern is instructive: agreements that address the parties' underlying concerns have proven markedly more stable than those imposed by determination. It remains this office's position that the objective is not the assignment of resources by fiat, but the creation of conditions in which the parties themselves arrive at an allocation each can sustain.
authentic_text.source: Illustrative internal dispute resolution memorandum, modelled on formal HR and project governance practices in large organisations
authentic_text.notes: The memorandum uses carefully hedged, formally inclusive language to frame a potentially adversarial situation as a collaborative problem-solving opportunity — a defining feature of institutional conflict resolution communication.

critical_reading.question: What does the independent review identify as the key difference between the parties' stated positions and their underlying interests?
critical_reading.answer: While their stated positions appear irreconcilable, their underlying interests substantially overlap: both divisions are primarily concerned with project continuity, managing stakeholder risk, and demonstrating departmental capability within budget constraints.

critical_reading.question: What does the phrase 'failure to engage with this process will be noted' imply in the context of a voluntary process?
critical_reading.answer: It implies that while participation is framed as voluntary, non-participation carries implicit consequences — the phrase functions as a veiled warning that non-engagement will be viewed unfavourably if the dispute escalates further. The 'voluntary' framing is therefore partially rhetorical.

critical_reading.question: Describe the overall tone of the memorandum and identify two phrases that are particularly characteristic of this tone.
critical_reading.answer: The tone is formally neutral and constructively diplomatic — it carefully avoids assigning blame or taking sides. 'Issued in the spirit of constructive dialogue' and 'does not represent a determination of any party's position' are characteristic: they signal institutional impartiality and reframe the intervention as facilitation rather than adjudication.

critical_reading.question: The term 'positional bargaining' in the proposed framework section refers to:
critical_reading.answer: A negotiation approach in which each party takes a fixed position (a stated demand or offer) and bargains from that position, rather than exploring the underlying needs or interests that the position is meant to satisfy. It is contrasted here with 'interest-based discussion.'

critical_reading.question: Why does the memorandum state that its goal is 'not to impose a resolution but to create the conditions in which one can be found'?
critical_reading.answer: This framing serves two purposes: it reduces defensiveness by reassuring both parties that they will retain agency in the resolution process, and it positions the dispute resolution office as a facilitator rather than an arbiter — reducing the likelihood that either party will resist engagement.

critical_reading.question: What three principles will govern the facilitated dialogue, and what is the purpose of the 'without prejudice' principle?
critical_reading.answer: The discussion will be interest-based rather than positional; contributions will be treated as exploratory and 'without prejudice'; and the facilitator's role is expressly non-adjudicative. The without-prejudice principle ensures that 'no proposal offered in the spirit of problem-solving may later be cited as a concession of position' — protecting parties so they can explore accommodations freely without fear it will weaken them in any later escalation.

critical_reading.question: Why does the memorandum make confidentiality 'a condition of the process', and how is this linked to candour?
critical_reading.answer: Because parties are more willing to explore accommodations and acknowledge the legitimacy of an opposing interest when assured it will not be used against them if the matter escalates. Confidentiality removes the strategic risk of openness, creating the psychological safety needed for genuine problem-solving rather than defensive posturing — candour depends on the guarantee that candour carries no penalty.

critical_reading.question: What does the 'Note on Precedent' contribute to the memorandum's persuasive purpose?
critical_reading.answer: It supplies evidence that the interest-based approach works, citing two comparable disputes in eighteen months where facilitated dialogue produced durable agreements that positional escalation had failed to reach. By showing that interest-based agreements 'have proven markedly more stable than those imposed', it reassures reluctant parties that the process is not untested idealism but a demonstrated method, strengthening the invitation to participate in good faith.

critical_reading.question: How does the memorandum's register sustain neutrality between the disputing divisions, and why is that neutrality strategically important?
critical_reading.answer: It uses impersonal, procedural, hedged language ('participants are asked to', 'it is a condition of the process', 'this office's position'), avoids attributing fault to either division, and repeatedly stresses that the facilitator is non-adjudicative and imposes nothing. This scrupulous neutrality is strategic because a dispute-resolution office that appeared to favour one side would forfeit the trust on which voluntary participation depends; the register itself is doing the work of keeping both parties willing to engage.

language_analysis.focus: Tentative Language in Professional Conflict and Difficult Conversations
language_analysis.explanation:
Tentative language encompasses a range of grammatical and lexical devices that soften the force of assertions, proposals, and criticisms in sensitive professional contexts. It includes modal verbs of low probability or possibility ('might,' 'may,' 'could'), hedging adverbs ('perhaps,' 'arguably,' 'to some extent'), distancing expressions ('it would seem,' 'there appears to be'), and embedded conditionals ('if I understand correctly,' 'should this prove to be the case'). These devices are particularly essential in professional conflict, where the stakes of communicative directness are high.

Tentative language is not a sign of weakness or indecision; at C1/C2 level, it is deployed strategically by sophisticated communicators who understand that direct accusation or demand triggers defensive reactions that obstruct resolution. By introducing a potentially unwelcome point tentatively ('I wonder whether there might be a misunderstanding around the scope of responsibilities'), the speaker opens a conversational door without pushing the other party through it by force.

The key professional skill is calibrating tentativeness appropriately: too much produces vagueness and signals that the speaker can be ignored; too little produces confrontation. The memorandum above models this calibration carefully — the language is formal and hedged throughout, but the warning embedded in 'failure to engage... will be noted' is unmistakably firm.

examples.from_text: it would seem that the stated positions of the two parties appear irreconcilable
examples.analysis: Three layers of tentativeness operate simultaneously: 'it would seem' is an impersonal distancing construction; 'appear' is a perception verb rather than a certainty verb; 'irreconcilable' is strong, but its force is absorbed by the surrounding tentativeness. The effect is that a stark finding is communicated without attribution or confrontation.

examples.from_text: Experience from comparable disputes suggests that when parties shift from positional bargaining to interest-based discussion, the range of viable solutions expands considerably.
examples.analysis: 'Suggests' (rather than 'proves' or 'demonstrates') is a hedging reporting verb. The claim is framed as an empirical observation rather than a prescription, which makes it more difficult for a defensive reader to reject it as interference.

contrast.formal: I wonder whether it might be worth revisiting how responsibilities were allocated at the project outset, as there may be some ambiguity that has contributed to the current situation.
contrast.informal: You took on work that wasn't yours and now there's a big problem because of it.

contrast.formal: It would appear that our respective understandings of the deliverable scope have diverged somewhat from the original agreement.
contrast.informal: You clearly don't understand what we agreed at the beginning.

error_correction.instruction: Each sentence contains one subtle error typical of advanced learners in professional contexts. Identify and correct it.

sentences.incorrect: I would like to raise a concern with regards of the way this situation has been handled.
sentences.correct: I would like to raise a concern with regard to the way this situation has been handled.
sentences.explanation: The correct fixed expression is 'with regard to' (singular, followed by 'to'). 'With regards of' conflates two different expressions: 'with regard to' and 'as regards.' 'With regards to' (plural) is widely used but considered non-standard in formal writing — 'with regard to' is preferred.

sentences.incorrect: The conflict has arisen due to a misunderstanding from both parties about their respective roles.
sentences.correct: The conflict has arisen due to a misunderstanding on the part of both parties about their respective roles.
sentences.explanation: 'A misunderstanding from both parties' uses 'from' incorrectly in this context. The standard formal expressions are 'on the part of both parties' or 'between both parties.' 'From' implies origin of a communication, not attribution of responsibility.

sentences.incorrect: She raised the issue to her line manager immediately after the meeting had taken place.
sentences.correct: She raised the issue with her line manager immediately after the meeting had taken place.
sentences.explanation: The verb 'raise' in the sense of bringing something to someone's attention takes the preposition 'with,' not 'to.' 'Raised the issue with her line manager' is the correct professional collocation. 'Raised it to' is a common preposition error.

sentences.incorrect: If the two departments would communicate more openly, many of these disputes could be avoided.
sentences.correct: If the two departments communicated more openly, many of these disputes could be avoided.
sentences.explanation: In second conditional sentences expressing hypothetical present situations, the if-clause uses the past simple — not 'would.' Using 'would' in the if-clause is a very common and persistent error among advanced learners.

debate_task.motion: This house believes that professional disagreement should always be resolved through formal mediation processes rather than direct negotiation between the parties involved
key_arguments: Formal mediation provides a structured, impartial framework that prevents the power imbalances inherent in direct negotiation from determining the outcome — particularly important where one party has significantly more organisational authority.

Mediated processes create a documented record of the dispute and its resolution, which provides legal and procedural protection for both parties and the organisation in the event of future escalation.

Where interpersonal trust has been significantly damaged, direct negotiation is unlikely to produce durable agreement; a neutral facilitator can create conditions for resolution that the parties cannot generate between themselves.
counter_arguments: Formal mediation is resource-intensive, slow, and often disproportionate to the scale of most workplace disagreements; encouraging direct resolution builds professional resilience and interpersonal competence that has wider organisational value.

Introducing a formal process can entrench conflict by formalising adversarial positions — many disputes that could have been resolved informally become more intractable once they enter institutional channels.

In high-trust, high-performance team cultures, the expectation of direct, candid communication is itself a cultural value; routing conflicts through formal mediation can be perceived as a failure of leadership and an admission of relational breakdown.
discourse_markers: While it is true that... nevertheless,
debate_task.task: Write a 2-minute speech arguing FOR or AGAINST the motion. Engage with the complexity of different workplace contexts and avoid making absolute claims unsupported by reasoning.

extended_writing.task: You are a senior team leader. Two members of your team — both capable professionals — have come into direct conflict over credit for a client project, with each claiming primary authorship of a proposal that won a major contract. The conflict has become visible to the rest of the team and is affecting morale. Write a formal email to both parties (addressed together) proposing a structured conversation, acknowledging both perspectives, and setting out your expectations for how the situation will be resolved.

structure.guidance: Open by naming the situation directly but without assigning blame. Acknowledge that both parties have a legitimate perspective and that you understand why the situation has arisen.
Briefly note the impact of the visible conflict on the wider team and on the professional environment. Keep this factual and non-punitive — describe the observable effect, not a character judgement.

Set out your proposal for how the situation will be addressed. Be specific about the format (individual conversations first, then a facilitated three-way meeting). Frame this as a structured opportunity, not a disciplinary measure.
State clearly but diplomatically what you expect from both parties going forward. Close warmly but firmly, reaffirming your confidence in both individuals and your commitment to a fair resolution.

extended_writing.model_answer:
Subject: Project Gamma Proposal — Let's Resolve This Together

Dear Priya and Daniel,

I am writing to you jointly because I believe it is important that both of you receive the same message from me at the same time. I am aware that there is a significant disagreement between you regarding the respective contributions to the Hartley proposal, and I want to address it directly and constructively.

I want to be clear that I do not doubt either of your commitment to this project, nor am I in a position to adjudicate this dispute based solely on the accounts I have heard so far. What I can say is that the disagreement — as it has played out over the past week — has been visible to the wider team and is creating an environment that is difficult for everyone. That is not a sustainable situation, and I do not think either of you intends it.

I would like to arrange individual conversations with each of you separately, beginning tomorrow, to ensure I fully understand your respective perspectives before we meet together. Following those conversations, I am proposing a facilitated three-way meeting — with HR present if either of you would find that helpful — in which we work towards a shared account of the project and a clear plan for how collaborative credit is attributed going forward.

I expect both of you to engage with this process in good faith and to maintain professional conduct with each other and the team while it proceeds. I have every confidence that this can be resolved.

With best regards,
Ahmed Hassan
Senior Team Lead

advanced_grammar.structure: Ellipsis in Professional Speech and Formal Writing
advanced_grammar.explanation:
Ellipsis is the deliberate omission of words or phrases that can be recovered from context, creating economy of expression without loss of meaning. In professional communication, ellipsis operates at multiple levels: grammatical ellipsis (omission of repeated grammatical elements), lexical ellipsis (omission of recoverable nouns or verbs), and discourse ellipsis (omission of elements recoverable from the wider communicative context).

In formal professional writing, ellipsis is most commonly encountered in parallel structures and contrastive pairs, where repeated elements are omitted to create rhetorical crispness and emphasis. For example: 'Some employees prefer direct feedback; others [prefer] written summaries.' The omitted 'prefer' is recoverable from the first clause. More advanced uses of ellipsis create powerful rhetorical effects in speeches and formal documents: 'Our goal is not to impose a resolution but [our goal is] to create the conditions in which one can be found.'

In professional conflict and negotiation contexts, ellipsis also appears in spoken dialogue as a signal of sophistication and collaborative engagement — responding to a point with 'Agreed on the timeline; less so on [the] resources' is a more precise and confident communicative act than a fully explicit restatement. Mastery of ellipsis marks a speaker or writer as genuinely operating at C2 level in professional discourse.
authentic_examples: The Technology Division has submitted its position; Operations, theirs. Neither is fully satisfactory.
Some disputes require formal mediation; most do not — and knowing which is which is among the most valuable professional skills a leader can develop.
Our role is not to judge who was right, but to ensure that whatever the outcome, the relationship — and the team — remain intact.

practice.sentence: Some managers prefer to address conflict immediately. Other managers prefer to allow a cooling-off period before they address conflict.
practice.transform: Reduce using ellipsis to eliminate unnecessary repetition.
practice.answer: Some managers prefer to address conflict immediately; others [prefer to allow] a cooling-off period first.

practice.sentence: The goal of this process is not to determine who was at fault. The goal of this process is to establish how we prevent the same situation from arising again.
practice.transform: Reduce using ellipsis, preserving the contrastive structure.
practice.answer: The goal of this process is not to determine who was at fault, but to establish how we prevent the same situation from arising again.

practice.sentence: Both parties have presented their accounts. Both accounts have merit, but both accounts are also incomplete.
practice.transform: Use ellipsis to create a more rhetorically powerful version.
practice.answer: Both parties have presented their accounts — each with merit, each incomplete.

quiz.question: What does the dispute resolution memorandum identify as the key insight from the independent review?
options: That one division is clearly in the wrong and should concede its position
That while the stated positions appear irreconcilable, the underlying interests substantially overlap
That the dispute cannot be resolved without senior management arbitration
That the project should be cancelled due to unresolvable resourcing conflict
quiz.explanation: The memorandum explicitly states that 'the underlying interests they seek to protect are substantially overlapping' despite apparently irreconcilable positions — this is the foundational insight of interest-based dispute resolution.

quiz.question: Which sentence correctly uses ellipsis to create a rhetorically crisp professional statement?
options: The Operations team wants more resources and the Technology team also wants more resources.
Both teams want more resources; neither has them.
Operations wants resources and Technology wants resources and they are both lacking resources.
The Operations team and the Technology team both want resources and both of them are lacking those resources.
quiz.explanation: 'Both teams want more resources; neither has them' uses ellipsis to eliminate repeated elements ('wants more resources / has them'), creating a crisp, emphatic contrast that is far more rhetorically powerful than the fully explicit alternatives.

quiz.question: Identify the error in the conditional sentence: 'If the two departments would communicate more openly, many disputes could be avoided.'
options: The main clause should use 'will' instead of 'could'
The if-clause should use the past simple ('communicated'), not 'would communicate'
The subject should be singular: 'the two departments communicates'
There is no error — the sentence is grammatically correct
quiz.explanation: In second conditional sentences expressing present hypothetical situations, the if-clause uses the past simple ('communicated'). Using 'would' in the if-clause is one of the most persistent errors among advanced learners.

quiz.question: What is the rhetorical purpose of framing participation in the mediation as 'voluntary' while simultaneously warning that non-participation 'will be noted'?
options: To confuse the parties about their legal obligations
To preserve the appearance of voluntary engagement while creating implicit pressure to participate
To avoid the legal requirement to make mediation compulsory
To signal that the dispute resolution office is indifferent to whether the parties engage
quiz.explanation: The 'voluntary but noted' formulation is a classic institutional hedging device: it maintains the collaborative framing ('voluntary') that is necessary for productive engagement, while ensuring parties understand there are consequences for non-participation.

quiz.question: Which sentence demonstrates the correct use of tentative language appropriate to professional conflict communication?
options: You clearly misunderstood the scope of the project from the very beginning.
I think maybe you might perhaps not have fully understood the scope.
I wonder whether there may have been some ambiguity in how the project scope was communicated at the outset.
The scope was not misunderstood by you, was it?
quiz.explanation: 'I wonder whether there may have been some ambiguity' uses calibrated tentativeness: 'I wonder whether' signals a question rather than an accusation; 'may have been' uses a possibility modal; 'some ambiguity' is less charged than 'misunderstanding.' The passive 'was communicated' distributes rather than assigns responsibility.

listening_exercises.transcript: Principled negotiation, developed at the Harvard Negotiation Project, rests on four commitments: separate the people from the problem; focus on interests, not positions; generate options before deciding; and insist on objective criteria. The genius of the fourth is that it depersonalizes disagreement. 'I want more' invites a contest of wills. 'Let's look at what comparable roles pay in this market' invites joint problem-solving. When both sides argue from standards, conceding to evidence is not losing face — it is being reasonable. Let me draw out why the fourth commitment — insisting on objective criteria — is the quiet masterstroke of principled negotiation, because it solves a problem the other three cannot fully reach. Even after you have separated the people from the problem, focused on interests, and generated options, you eventually face the moment of decision: whose number, whose split, whose version wins? If that moment becomes a contest of wills — I want more, no I want more — you are back in positional bargaining, and the party with more stubbornness or more power prevails, leaving the loser resentful and the agreement fragile. Objective criteria dissolve this. Instead of pitting one will against another, both parties turn to an external standard that neither controls: market data, an independent valuation, industry benchmarks, precedent, a professional's assessment. 'I want a higher salary' invites a fight; 'let's look at what comparable roles with my qualifications pay in this market' invites joint inquiry. Notice the transformation. Once the conversation is anchored to an external standard, conceding is no longer a defeat of your will by theirs — it is simply being reasonable in the face of evidence, and being reasonable costs no face at all. This is why skilled negotiators invest heavily, before the conversation, in finding the fair standards that apply: the party who arrives with credible objective criteria largely sets the terms of the discussion, not by force but by framing. And when both sides accept that the question is 'what does the evidence support?' rather than 'who can outlast whom?', you have converted a battle into a shared problem — and shared problems produce agreements that hold, because each party can defend the outcome to their own side as fair rather than merely as the best they could extract.
listening_exercises.question: What is the benefit of insisting on objective criteria?
options: It guarantees you win
It depersonalizes disagreement into joint problem-solving
It shortens meetings
It avoids all conflict

listening_exercises.transcript: Mediating a dispute between colleagues, resist the referee role — you are not there to declare a winner. Open by establishing common ground: both parties want the project to succeed. Have each side state the other's position to the other's satisfaction before advocating their own; this single step dissolves most manufactured disagreements, which turn out to be misunderstandings wearing armor. Then move the conversation from the past, which cannot be negotiated, to the future, which can: 'What would working well together look like from Monday?' When you are asked to mediate between two colleagues, the deepest instinct — and the one you must resist hardest — is to become a referee: to hear both sides, decide who is right, and announce a verdict. Do not. The moment you declare a winner, you have created a loser who will not honour the outcome and who now resents you as well as their opponent. Your job is not to judge the dispute but to change the conditions under which the parties address it. Begin by establishing common ground, however basic — 'I think we can agree that we all want this project to succeed and none of us wants to be having this conversation again in a month.' That shared floor matters, because it reminds two people who feel like adversaries that they are, in fact, on the same side of a larger goal. Then deploy the single most powerful move in conflict resolution: before either party is allowed to argue their own case, require each to state the other's position to the other's satisfaction. This is harder than it sounds and more transformative than it looks. To restate your opponent's view well enough that they say 'yes, that's what I mean', you have to actually listen to it, and the act of being genuinely heard visibly lowers people's defences. More than that: an astonishing proportion of workplace disputes turn out, under this exercise, to be not real disagreements at all but misunderstandings wearing armour — two people who actually want compatible things but have been talking past each other, each reacting to a caricature of the other's position rather than the position itself. Strip away the caricature by forcing genuine restatement, and much of the conflict simply evaporates. Only then, with defences lowered and misunderstandings cleared, do you turn the conversation from the past — which is fixed, and can only be re-litigated — to the future, which is the only thing anyone can actually negotiate: 'So, starting Monday, what would working well together actually look like?'
listening_exercises.question: What does having each side restate the other's position accomplish?
options: It determines who is right
It dissolves disagreements that are really misunderstandings
It creates a written record
It saves time

speaking_task.context: Two members of your team disagree about ownership of a project, and both have come to you. You have called a joint meeting.
speaking_task.prompt: Record your opening two minutes as mediator: establish common ground, set the restating rule, and move the conversation from past grievances to future working agreements.
useful_language: We're here because both of you want this project to succeed.
Before we discuss solutions, I'll ask each of you to state the other's position — to their satisfaction.
The past we can learn from; only the future is negotiable.
What would working well together look like from Monday?
Let's write down what we agree on.
speaking_task.model_answer: Thanks for coming, both of you. I want to start with what's not in dispute: you both want this launch to succeed, and frankly it needs you both. Here's how we'll run this. Before anyone argues their own case, I'll ask each of you to state the other's position — and we'll check that the restatement is fair. Sara, you'll summarize David's view first; David, you'll do the same. In my experience, half of what looks like disagreement dissolves at this step. Then we're going to point forward: the past we can learn from, but only the future is negotiable. The question on the table is not who was right in March; it's what ownership looks like from Monday. And whatever we agree, we write down before we leave the room.

writing_workshop.task: Write a mediation summary memo after a workplace dispute (real or invented): neutral statement of each party's interests, the agreements reached, and the objective criteria that will judge success — without assigning blame for the past.
writing_workshop.model_text: Memo: Resolution summary — reporting-line question, data team. Context: Sara and David each understood themselves to own the client dashboard, an ambiguity created when the project moved departments in March. Interests: Sara's priority is design consistency with the analytics suite she maintains; David's is delivery speed for a client he faces weekly. Both stated the other's interest to the other's satisfaction in our meeting of the 14th. Agreements: Sara owns the dashboard's architecture and review; David owns client requirements and release scheduling; changes touching both require a same-day conversation, not an email chain. Success criteria: releases remain on the biweekly schedule, review turnaround stays under two working days, and the client's quarterly satisfaction score holds or improves. We will review against these three measures on January 15. No further account of the March transition is required from either party.
writing_workshop.model_analysis: The memo treats the dispute's origin as structural ('an ambiguity created when...'), records interests rather than accusations, and converts the resolution into three measurable criteria with a review date — turning peace into a checkable agreement.
success_criteria: Objective success criteria and a review date
No blame assigned for the past

note_taking.prompt: Note (1) why insisting on objective criteria is the key move in principled negotiation, and (2) the steps for mediating a dispute between colleagues. Compare with the model.
model_notes: Objective criteria depersonalise: 'what do comparable roles pay?' replaces a contest of wills → conceding to evidence isn't losing face
Mediating: resist the referee role; don't declare a winner (creates a loser who won't honour it)
Open with common ground; have each side restate the other's position to satisfaction first — dissolves misunderstandings
Move the conversation from the past (fixed) to the future ('what would working well look like from Monday?')
